title: From Business Question to Data Question

production_notes: No facts to verify: the bakery in Accra, Kwame and all figures are fictional (content.md Review Flags: None).
Kwame's sheet columns shown on slides: Month, Product, Units sold, Revenue (GHS), Ingredient cost (GHS). The script gives no profit figures for Kwame because content.md gives none.
The 5,000 / 6,000 revenue example in scene 5 matches content.md exactly.
Stock footage of the bakery must show no real shop names or logos.

Hook.voiceover: How is the shop doing? Every owner asks this question. But if you type it into an AI tool with your sales sheet, you get a long, general answer that does not help you decide anything. The problem is not the AI. The problem is the question.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, we made our files safe to upload. Now we make our questions clear, because good analysis starts with a clear question.

slide.title: From Business Question to Data Question
slide.body: AI-Powered Data Analysis (No Code) · Lesson 3 of 14

Explain.voiceover: A business question is what you or your manager want to know, in everyday words. Are we losing money? Is the new menu working? A data question is one that your spreadsheet can answer with a number.

slide.title: Two kinds of question
slide.body: Business question (everyday words): 'Are we losing money?' · 'Is the new menu working?' | Data question: answered with a number from your spreadsheet

Explain.voiceover: To turn a business question into data questions, make each one measurable with four parts. What to measure. Revenue, units, profit, or number of customers? Which group. All products, or one product? All shops, or one region? Which time period. Last month, this quarter, or January to April?

slide.title: Four parts of a data question
slide.body: Four tiles, first three lit: What to measure (revenue, units, profit, customers) · Which group (product, shop, region) · Which time period (last month, this quarter, Jan–Apr) · Compared with what? (dimmed)

Explain.voiceover: And the fourth part, compared with what? This is the one people forget most often. Revenue was five thousand in March means little on its own. Revenue was five thousand in March, against six thousand in February, tells you something.

slide.title: Compared with what?
slide.body: Left (grey): 'Revenue was 5,000 in March.' Right (teal): 'Revenue was 5,000 in March, against 6,000 in February.'

Explain.voiceover: Next, check that your data can answer each question. Name the columns you need. If a column does not exist, you need more data or a different question. You find missing data before you start the analysis, not after. And write your data questions before you open any AI tool.

slide.title: Name the columns
slide.body: Data question card → arrow → column headers ticked (green) or missing (red cross: 'need more data or a different question'). Footer: Write questions before opening AI.

Explain.voiceover: Here is a way to picture it. A business question is like telling a taxi driver, take me somewhere nice. A data question is like giving the exact address. Both start the journey, but only one gets you to a place you can check you have reached.
Explain.stock_query: passenger talking to taxi driver city
Explain.on_screen_text: Somewhere nice, or an exact address?

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's meet Kwame. He runs a bakery in Accra, Ghana, and he is worried. My profits are falling, he says. His fictional sales sheet has five columns. Month, product, units sold, revenue, and ingredient cost, both in Ghanaian cedis.
Demonstrate.stock_query: baker arranging fresh bread in bakery

Demonstrate.voiceover: Profits are falling is a feeling, not yet a question. So Kwame breaks it into three data questions. First, is profit really falling, and since when? He looks at profit per month, which is revenue minus ingredient cost, from January to June, month by month. He needs the month, revenue and ingredient cost columns.

slide.title: Question 1: Is profit really falling?
slide.body: Card 1: Profit per month (Revenue − Ingredient cost), January to June, month by month. Column tags: Month · Revenue · Ingredient cost

Demonstrate.voiceover: Second, is it all products, or only some? He compares each product's profit in January with its profit in June. This adds the product column.

slide.title: Question 2: All products or some?
slide.body: Card 2: Profit per product per month, each product's January vs June. Column tags: Product · Month · Revenue · Ingredient cost

Demonstrate.voiceover: Third, is it fewer sales, or higher costs? He compares units sold per month with ingredient cost per unit. That is ingredient cost divided by units sold.

slide.title: Question 3: Fewer sales or higher costs?
slide.body: Card 3: Units sold per month vs ingredient cost per unit (Ingredient cost ÷ Units sold). Column tags: Month · Units sold · Ingredient cost

Demonstrate.voiceover: The answers are clear. Total units are stable. But the ingredient cost per loaf of one bread type has risen since April. The worry, profits are falling, is now a specific finding he can act on. He can review the price or the recipe of one product.

slide.title: From worry to finding
slide.body: Left: 'My profits are falling' (vague). Right: Units stable (flat line) · Cost per loaf of one bread type up since April (rising line) → Action: review price or recipe of one product

Demonstrate.voiceover: Notice what Kwame did not ask. Why are customers unhappy? His sheet has no column about customer opinions, so that question needs different data.

A common mistake is to write data questions that are still vague, like look at sales trends. Ask yourself, could two people answer this question and get the same number? If not, it is not yet measurable. Add the measure, the group, the time period and the comparison.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a business question is what you want to know in everyday words. A data question can be answered with a number from your data. Second, make each data question measurable. What to measure, which group, which time period, and compared with what. Third, name the columns each question needs, so you discover missing data before you start.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Business question = everyday words; data question = a number. 2. Measure · group · time period · compared with what. 3. Name the columns before you start.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will write one business question from your own work, or use the sample café dataset, and break it into three measurable data questions, with the columns each one needs. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, we clean messy data with AI help. See you there.
